explanations.explanation: Yes, friend, a mighty king. The Teacher says he “…came against it, surrounded it, and built large siege ramps against it.” (Ecclesiastes 9:14) Few men inside, one big king outside. That is a lopsided day.
Giants get all the good stories, baker, but not this one. The Teacher says “A mighty king came against it…” (Ecclesiastes 9:14) The trouble here wears a crown.
Close to the right neighborhood, but the text has a different title in mind. It says “A mighty king came against it…” (Ecclesiastes 9:14) The one coming against the city is a king, not a commander.
That's the one. “Now a poor wise man was found in the city, and he saved the city by his wisdom.” (Ecclesiastes 9:15) Wisdom did the saving. I like that, because wisdom doesn't need a big budget.
I can see why a little hero would come to mind. But this passage names a different rescuer: a poor wise man. “…he saved the city by his wisdom.” (Ecclesiastes 9:15) Wisdom is what the text credits.
Not this time, baker. The text says the man was poor, not rich. He was a poor wise man, and he saved the city by his wisdom (Ecclesiastes 9:15). His wallet had nothing to do with it.

It would be nice if that were true, wouldn't it? But the text says the opposite: “Yet no one remembered that poor man.” (Ecclesiastes 9:15) He saved the whole city, and still no one remembered him. That one stings.

Right, it's false. He saved the city by his wisdom, “Yet no one remembered that poor man.” (Ecclesiastes 9:15) Saving a whole city and not being remembered is hard to hear. I know a little about being forgotten, and I think the Teacher is noticing something real.

explanations.answer: People despise it and ignore his words
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The Teacher says “Wisdom is better than strength, but the wisdom of the poor man is despised, and his words are not heeded.” (Ecclesiastes 9:16) Wisdom wins, yet the man holding it gets the cold shoulder. Both things are true at once.

explanations.answer: Kings write it down to use later
explanations.explanation: That would be a happy ending, but the text doesn't give us one. It says “…the wisdom of the poor man is despised, and his words are not heeded.” (Ecclesiastes 9:16) Being heeded is exactly what the verse says is missing.

explanations.answer: The city pays him gold to hear it
explanations.explanation: Nice thought, friend, and I'd love to see that line at the bank. But the text says “…the wisdom of the poor man is despised, and his words are not heeded.” (Ecclesiastes 9:16) The verse has people not listening to him.
Yes, true, baker. “The calm words of the wise are heeded over the shouts of a ruler among fools.” (Ecclesiastes 9:17) Calm beats loud in this verse. And I say that as a stamper who loves being loud.

It's actually true, and the verse says it plainly. “The calm words of the wise are heeded over the shouts of a ruler among fools.” (Ecclesiastes 9:17) The shouting ruler doesn't win this one. Quiet wisdom does.
That's the word. “Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner destroys much good.” (Ecclesiastes 9:18) One person can wreck a lot. It's a little like one dropped tray ruining a whole batch.
That would be a nicer line, but it isn't this one. The verse says “…one sinner destroys much good.” (Ecclesiastes 9:18) The word is destroys.
I wish that were the word, baker. But the verse goes the other direction: “…one sinner destroys much good.” (Ecclesiastes 9:18) It has one sinner tearing down, not building up.

explanations.answer: A little folly outweighs wisdom and honor
explanations.explanation: That's the point. “As dead flies bring a stench to the perfumer’s oil, so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor.” (Ecclesiastes 10:1) The dead flies bring a stench to the oil. A little folly does the same to wisdom and honor.

explanations.answer: A little wisdom outweighs folly and shame
explanations.explanation: That one is flipped around, friend. The verse says “…a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor.” (Ecclesiastes 10:1) The flies are folly, and the oil is wisdom and honor.

explanations.answer: Great honor covers over a little folly
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but the flies win in this picture. The Teacher says “…a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor.” (Ecclesiastes 10:1) The folly isn't covered up, it brings the stench.

I bet he'd love that, but the text says otherwise. “Even as the fool walks along the road, his sense is lacking, and he shows everyone that he is a fool.” (Ecclesiastes 10:3) The verse says he shows everyone. Nobody gets left out of that picture.
Right, it's false. The fool walks down the road, “…his sense is lacking, and he shows everyone that he is a fool.” (Ecclesiastes 10:3) He isn't hiding anything. He's basically wearing a sign.

Yes, calmness, baker. “If the ruler’s temper flares against you, do not abandon your post, for calmness lays great offenses to rest.” (Ecclesiastes 10:4) The ruler's temper is hot, so the answer is the opposite. Stay steady where you are.

I get it, distance sounds safe. But the verse says the opposite: “…do not abandon your post, for calmness lays great offenses to rest.” (Ecclesiastes 10:4) Staying put and staying calm is the word here.
A gift basket would be a creative idea, baker. But the verse says “…calmness lays great offenses to rest.” (Ecclesiastes 10:4) Nothing in it mentions gifts.

explanations.answer: Slaves on horseback and princes on foot
explanations.explanation: That's what he saw. “I have seen slaves on horseback, while princes go on foot like slaves.” (Ecclesiastes 10:7) The Teacher calls it an evil he has seen under the sun, an error from the ruler (Ecclesiastes 10:5). Everything is flipped.

explanations.answer: Priests in fields and farmers in temples
explanations.explanation: That's a good flipped picture, but it isn't his. The Teacher says “I have seen slaves on horseback, while princes go on foot like slaves.” (Ecclesiastes 10:7) Horses and feet are the details.

explanations.answer: Soldiers at feasts and kings at the gate
explanations.explanation: Interesting scene, friend, but he doesn't describe it. What he saw was “…slaves on horseback, while princes go on foot like slaves.” (Ecclesiastes 10:7) Folks on horses, folks on foot, and it's all backward.

True, baker. “The one who quarries stones may be injured by them, and he who splits logs endangers himself.” (Ecclesiastes 10:9) Every job has its risks, even the ones that look simple. Splitting logs is right there on the Teacher's list. Let's all respect the log splitters.
It's actually true, baker. The verse says “…he who splits logs endangers himself.” (Ecclesiastes 10:9) Hard work comes with real risk.

That's right, skill. “If the axe is dull and the blade unsharpened, more strength must be exerted, but skill produces success.” (Ecclesiastes 10:10) Pushing harder isn't the same as working smarter. The sharp thinking does the job.
Fast feels like progress, but it isn't the word here. The verse says “…skill produces success.” (Ecclesiastes 10:10) A fast swing with a dull axe is still a dull axe.

Size sounds like it could help, but the verse names something else. “If the axe is dull and the blade unsharpened, more strength must be exerted, but skill produces success.” (Ecclesiastes 10:10) A dull axe calls for more strength. Skill is what produces success.
That would be a rough business model, friend. The verse says “If the snake bites before it is charmed, there is no profit for the charmer.” (Ecclesiastes 10:11) Too late means nothing gained.

Right, it's false, baker. “If the snake bites before it is charmed, there is no profit for the charmer.” (Ecclesiastes 10:11) When the bite comes first, the charmer gets no profit. Timing matters, and he comes up empty.

Yes, consume, baker. “The words of a wise man’s mouth are gracious, but the lips of a fool consume him.” (Ecclesiastes 10:12) Gracious words on one side, consuming lips on the other. A fool's own talk eats him up.
That'd be handy, but it's not the word. The verse says “…the lips of a fool consume him.” (Ecclesiastes 10:12) His words end up hurting him.
A nice idea, baker, but the verse goes the other way. “…the lips of a fool consume him.” (Ecclesiastes 10:12) The wise man's words are the ones called gracious. Honor isn't the word here.

explanations.answer: Starts foolish and ends even worse
explanations.explanation: That's the path. “The beginning of his talk is folly, and the end of his speech is evil madness.” (Ecclesiastes 10:13) It starts bad and gets worse. Keep talking and the hole gets deeper.

explanations.answer: Starts foolish and ends up wise
explanations.explanation: That would be a nice turnaround, but the verse doesn't give us one. It says “…the end of his speech is evil madness.” (Ecclesiastes 10:13) He doesn't get wiser as he goes.

explanations.answer: Starts wise and ends up foolish
explanations.explanation: Close, because it does end badly. But the verse says the beginning is already folly: “The beginning of his talk is folly, and the end of his speech is evil madness.” (Ecclesiastes 10:13) Foolish from the start, and worse at the end.

Not quite, baker. The verse says “No one knows what is coming, and who can tell him what will come after him?” (Ecclesiastes 10:14) The question hints that no one can tell him. The fool keeps talking anyway.

Right, false, baker. “No one knows what is coming, and who can tell him what will come after him?” (Ecclesiastes 10:14) The question leaves the fool with no one to tell him. Nobody can see ahead, and the fool still multiplies words.

explanations.answer: He does not know the way to the city
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, friend. “The toil of a fool wearies him, for he does not know the way to the city.” (Ecclesiastes 10:15) The text says he toils and he does not know the way. I bet that is exhausting.

explanations.answer: He carries heavy stones for the king
explanations.explanation: That does sound tiring, but the text gives a different reason. “The toil of a fool wearies him, for he does not know the way to the city.” (Ecclesiastes 10:15) The reason is not knowing the way. Stones and a king aren't mentioned in this verse.

explanations.answer: He works all night without any rest
explanations.explanation: Long nights are tiring, friend, but the verse doesn't say that. It says “…he does not know the way to the city.” (Ecclesiastes 10:15) He's worn out because he's lost.

explanations.answer: For strength and not for drunkenness
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. “Blessed are you, O land whose king is a son of nobles, and whose princes feast at the proper time—for strength and not for drunkenness.” (Ecclesiastes 10:17) The princes feast at the proper time, and it's for strength. The verse calls that land blessed.

explanations.answer: For praise and not for peace
explanations.explanation: Sounds fancy, baker, but those words aren't in the verse. The princes feast “…for strength and not for drunkenness.” (Ecclesiastes 10:17) Praise and peace didn't make the guest list. The verse keeps it simple, and I like simple.

explanations.answer: For show and not for hunger
explanations.explanation: Close, friend, but the verse says something else. The princes feast at the proper time “…for strength and not for drunkenness.” (Ecclesiastes 10:17) Show isn't on the list. I once set out a cookie box so fancy that nobody wanted to touch it, and a cookie nobody eats is just a very expensive coaster. Strength is the reason, and the verse calls that land blessed.

Yes, laziness, baker. “Through laziness the roof caves in, and in the hands of the idle, the house leaks.” (Ecclesiastes 10:18) The verse puts laziness right at the cause. Little jobs left undone add up, and the roof gives out.
That's the second blank. “…in the hands of the idle, the house leaks.” (Ecclesiastes 10:18) Idle hands, leaky house. The drip adds up.
Storms feel like a fair guess, baker. But the verse says the cause is laziness: “Through laziness the roof caves in…” (Ecclesiastes 10:18) It doesn't mention weather.
The wise are on the other side of this one. The verse says “…in the hands of the idle, the house leaks.” (Ecclesiastes 10:18) Idle is the word.
Money isn't the point of this line, friend. The house leaks “…in the hands of the idle…” (Ecclesiastes 10:18) It's about being idle, not being rich.

explanations.answer: A bird of the air may carry your words
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. “Do not curse the king even in your thoughts, or curse the rich even in your bedroom, for a bird of the air may carry your words, and a winged creature may report your speech.” (Ecclesiastes 10:20) Even private words can travel. The verse names a bird of the air and a winged creature.

explanations.answer: A servant at the door may hear your words
explanations.explanation: A sneaky servant would be a good guess, but it's not what the verse says. The reason is “…a bird of the air may carry your words…” (Ecclesiastes 10:20) Even the sky has ears.

explanations.answer: A guard at the gate may report your words
explanations.explanation: That sounds believable, baker, but the Teacher says something else. “…a bird of the air may carry your words, and a winged creature may report your speech.” (Ecclesiastes 10:20) The reporters in this verse have wings. Guards don't come into it.
